subject: Vocabulary
topic: Commonly Confused Words — Usage and Meaning (Set W7)

questions.stem:
Choose the sentence in which the word is used CORRECTLY:
(affect vs. effect)

options.option_text: The cold weather effected my mood negatively.
The medicine had a calming affect on the patient.
Pollution affects the quality of air in urban areas.
She effected a great change in the company's culture.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Affect' is a VERB meaning 'to influence'. 'Effect' is a NOUN meaning 'result/outcome'. So: 'Pollution AFFECTS air' (verb) is correct. Option A wrongly uses 'effected' (should be 'affected'). Option B wrongly uses 'affect' as a noun. Note: 'Effect' CAN be a verb, but only in formal contexts meaning 'to bring about' (as in option D, which is actually grammatically correct but rarely used — examiners prefer C for clarity).

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct word:
'The principal asked all students to _____ the assembly rules at all times.'
(accept / except)

options.option_text: except
accepted
accept
excepting

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Accept' means 'to agree to' or 'to follow'. 'Except' means 'excluding'. The sentence means the students should follow the rules. Memory tip: acCEPT = take/receive (you ACCEPT an offer). exCEPT = excluding (everyone EXCEPT him).

questions.stem:
Choose the sentence in which the word is used CORRECTLY:
(principal vs. principle)

options.option_text: Honesty is the principle value in his family.
She was the principle dancer in the troupe.
Our company operates on strict ethical principles.
The bank principal refers to the interest paid on loans.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Principles' = fundamental rules/values. 'Principal' = main person (school head) OR the main amount in finance. Memory: princiPAL = your PAL the head teacher. principlE = a rulE. Options A and B use 'principle' where 'principal' is needed. Option D confuses the finance meanings.

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct word:
'The car came to a _____ stop outside the store.'
(stationary / stationery)

options.option_text: stationery
stationarry
stationary
stationairy

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Stationary' (adjective) = not moving. 'Stationery' (noun) = paper, pens, and writing materials. Memory: stationERY = papER (both end in -ery/-er). stationARY = stAY (not moving — the 'a' stands still).

questions.stem:
Choose the sentence in which the word is used CORRECTLY:
(complement vs. compliment)

options.option_text: The teacher gave the student a generous complement on her essay.
Red wine complements a cheese platter perfectly.
She complimented her wardrobe with a colourful scarf.
He felt flattered by the complement from his boss.

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Complement' = to complete or go well with (adds something that makes a whole). 'Compliment' = to praise or flatter. 'Wine complements cheese' = they go well together. Memory: complEment = complEte. complIment = I like it (praise).

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct word:
'She gave me _____ to stay an extra hour at the gym.'
(advice / advise)

options.option_text: advise
adviced
advised
advice

questions.explanation: D is correct. 'Advice' (noun) = a recommendation or suggestion. 'Advise' (verb) = to give advice. 'She gave me advice' — the blank follows 'gave me', needing a noun. Memory: adVICE is NICE (both nouns). adVISE is what you DO (verb — the 's' sounds like 'z').

questions.stem:
Choose the sentence in which the word is used CORRECTLY:
(lose vs. loose)

options.option_text: I always loose my keys when I am in a hurry.
The runner was determined not to loose the race.
He wore a loose shirt to the picnic.
Don't lose that screw — it is very lose.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Loose' (adjective) = not tight, free. 'Lose' (verb) = to not win or to misplace. 'Loose shirt' = not tight-fitting. Options A and B use 'loose' where the verb 'lose' is needed. Option D uses 'lose' correctly first but then uses 'lose' again where 'loose' is needed.

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct word:
'The medicine was placed _____ the patient's reach on the top shelf.'
(beside / besides)

options.option_text: besides
beside
alongside
besides of

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Beside' = at the side of / next to (physical position). 'Besides' = in addition to, or moreover. 'Beyond the patient's reach' is the intended meaning, but 'beside the patient's reach' means placed next to/past the reach distance. The idiom 'beside oneself' and 'beside the point' use 'beside' for proximity. Here the intended meaning is near, so 'beside' is correct. 'Besides' would mean 'in addition to the patient's reach' — which doesn't make sense.

questions.stem:
Choose the sentence in which the word is used CORRECTLY:
(eminent vs. imminent)

options.option_text: The imminent scientist received a Nobel Prize last year.
The storm was eminent, with dark clouds gathering on the horizon.
An eminent judge was invited to speak at the law school's convocation.
Her retirement was imminent known to all her colleagues.

questions.explanation: C is correct. 'Eminent' = distinguished, well-respected, prominent in a field. 'Imminent' = about to happen soon. An 'eminent judge' = a respected/celebrated judge. Option A should be 'eminent' (a distinguished scientist). Option B should be 'imminent' (storm approaching soon). Option D is grammatically faulty — should be 'Her retirement was imminent, known to all...'

questions.stem:
Fill in the blank with the correct word:
'The magician created an _____ of a rabbit disappearing into thin air.'
(allusion / illusion)

options.option_text: allusion
illusion
elusion
allusory

questions.explanation: B is correct. 'Illusion' = a false perception or deceptive appearance (magician's trick). 'Allusion' = an indirect reference to something (literary/figurative). 'Elusion' = the act of avoiding — from 'elude'. Memory: ILLusion = tricks the eye (ILL = bad/misleading). ALLusion = ALL references to something cultural/literary.
